newsitem.title: UK: Coffee seen vulnerable as dazzling rally stalls.
newsitem.headline: Coffee seen vulnerable as dazzling rally stalls.

text.p: Coffee prices are tumbling, stalling a dazzling rally seen since the end of 1996, and analysts of the market say it looks vulnerable to more sell-offs at least in the short-term.

While the long-run fundamental outlook stays tight, because of worries about Latin American supply, the market is technically overbought and prone to selling by investment funds that are eager to lock in profits or cut losses.

By last week, coffee futures in New York and London had soared by around 50 percent from values traded late last year, driven by speculative and trade buying and led by a rollercoaster New York market.
The rise in the price of coffee beans triggered retail price rises for ground coffee in US and European supermarkets.
Prospects of a lower crop in Brazil and labour unrest in Colombia against a backdrop of low consumer stocks fuelled the rally.

The sharp and sudden jump in prices for high quality arabica beans, tradeed in New York, prompted some U.S. and European manufacturers, unable to contain soaring raw material costs, to hike retail prices or else include more relatively inferior robustas in their blend.
But since Friday, New York arabica futures have dropped as speculators took profits. London followed suit on Monday when New York was closed for a holiday.
The slide was extended to Tuesday, pushing the benchmark May robusta contract to $1,566 a tonne, a $49 loss on the day, by 1530 GMT.
May had peaked at $1,718 last week but the move above $1,700 proved to be shortlived.
Traders said an assumption that London had reached its peak would mirror views that New York had also reached a comfortable level and would start coming off from now on.

New York's May retreated sharply in early Tuesday trade on news of a resolution of an eight-day strike by 300,000 government workers in Colombia. By 1500 GMT, May was down 10.00 cents at 157 cents a lb.
Traders said roaster price-fixing ahead of New York's March first notice day later this week could limit the downside potential.
But the London market could induce fund selling if May, the centre of fund long positions, dives below $1,500.

"The funds have basically gone up the limit on the long side," one trader said. "The only thing they can do is to sell the market and start getting out. But whether they will take profit or losses remains to be seen."
"But the market is failing a bit at the moment," he added.
Fundamentally, supplies of the higher-quality arabica coffee are tight while robusta is sufficient to meet demand.
Analysts said concern about arabica supplies isn't likely to go away soon, They cite expectations of a lower Brazil 1997/98 crop, recent labour problems in Colombia and reduced Mexican output.
"The coffee market continued to soar and further explosive action could be seen not only in the weeks ahead but at least through mid-year," broker Merrill Lynch said in a report published last week.
Coffee prices began to climb after Brazil officials put the 1997/98 crop at below 20 million 60-kg bags against a market consensus of 23-24 million.
The surge escalated ahead of a late January meeting in Brazil of key producer nations aimed at further tightening a grip on coffee exports and locking in higher prices.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries said it would limit exports by a further 1.3 million bags in the first six months of 1997.

"Even if forecasts for a reduced Brazilian crop prove wrong, the problems in Colombia and elsewhere are acute enough to keep this market in a sustained uptrend," Merrill Lynch said. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
